title: Combining ratios
examples: How do I combine two separate ratios into one?
Is there a difference between a ratio and a fraction?
What if one of the ratios is already simplified?

explain.say: Today we are learning to combine ratios. We will learn how to find a single ratio from two smaller ones. This is useful when mixing ingredients.

draw.text: Combining Ratios: a:b and b:c → a:b:c

explain.say: If you know the ratio of apples to bananas is two to three. And you also know the ratio of bananas to cherries is three to five. Notice the common item here.
Because the banana part is three in both ratios, we can join them easily. The new combined ratio is apples to bananas to cherries.
Another example is the ratio of boys to girls is one to four. And the ratio of girls to teachers is four to one. The combined ratio is one to four to one.

faq.q: What if the common number is not the same in both ratios?
faq.a: If the common number is different, you must multiply the ratios to make the common number match. For example, if you have 2:3 and 4:3, you would scale the first ratio by 2.
asks: How do I adjust the ratios?
What if the middle term is different?

faq.q: Does combining ratios mean I have to simplify everything?
faq.a: No, combining ratios is about finding the overall relationship between three parts. You only simplify the final ratio if the numbers share a common factor.
asks: Do I simplify at the end?
When should I simplify the ratio?

faq.q: Can I use this method for ratios that don't share a common item?
faq.a: This specific method requires one item to be the second part in both ratios. If they do not share a common item, you must use different methods to combine them.
asks: What if there is no common link?
Does it always need a shared item?

faq.q: Is combining ratios the same as adding fractions?
faq.a: No, they are different concepts. Ratios show comparison, while fractions show parts of a whole. Combining ratios is about linking multiple comparisons.
asks: Is this like adding fractions together?

faq.q: What does it mean when I say a ratio is equivalent to a fraction?
faq.a: It means the ratio can be written as a fraction. For example, a ratio of two to five is the same as the fraction two divided by five.
asks: How is a ratio written as a fraction?
Can I write a ratio as a fraction?

facts: A ratio compares two quantities using a colon or the word 'to'.
A ratio of 'a' to 'b' can be written as a fraction a/b.
To combine ratios, the shared quantity must have the same value in both given ratios.
When combining ratios, you keep the common term's value consistent across all parts.

quiz.say: The ratio of cats to dogs is 3:5. The ratio of dogs to birds is 5:2. What is the combined ratio?
quiz.why: The dog part is five in both ratios, so you can directly combine them to get three to five to two.

wrong.1: This mistake happens if you simply add the two middle numbers together.
wrong.2: This mistake forgets to use the second ratio's final number.
wrong.3: This mistake suggests you should multiply everything first, which is not necessary here.

quiz.say: A recipe needs flour to sugar in a ratio of 4:3. It also needs sugar to butter in a ratio of 2:1. What is the combined ratio?
quiz.why: The sugar part needs to be the same. We multiply the first ratio by two to make the sugar part six, and the second ratio by three to make it six. Wait, the common term is sugar. In the first ratio it is three. In the second ratio it is two. We need the least common multiple of three and two, which is six. So, 4:3 becomes 8:6. And 2:1 becomes 6:3. The final ratio is 8:6:3.

wrong.0: This mistake only adjusts one of the ratios correctly.
wrong.2: This mistake ignores the need to make the common term equal.
wrong.3: This mistake incorrectly assumes the common term is five.

quiz.say: If the ratio of red paint to blue paint is 1:2, and the ratio of blue paint to yellow paint is 3:1. What is the combined ratio?
quiz.why: The blue paint needs to match. The first ratio has two, and the second has three. The smallest matching number is six. So the first ratio becomes three:six. The second ratio becomes nine:three. The final ratio is three:six:one.

wrong.1: This mistake ignores the need to scale the first ratio.
wrong.2: This mistake incorrectly assumes the second ratio's first number is the answer.
wrong.3: This mistake fails to simplify the final ratio.
